title: Artificial Intelligence in Neurology: A Critical Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence, Translation, and Responsible Implementation

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Artificial Intelligence in Neurology: A Critical Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence, Translation, and Responsible Implementation》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · brb371873-sec-0050-p1】Neurological disorders are a leading cause of global disability and mortality, creating substantial diagnostic, therapeutic, and health‐system burdens (GBD 2021 Nervous System Disorders Collaborators 2024; World Health Organization 2024; R. Yang et al. 2025; GBD 2021 Stroke Risk Factor Collaborators 2024). Their clinical heterogeneity and dependence on complex longitudinal data make neurology an important setting for evaluating AI, while also making overgeneralization especially hazardous.

【Introduction · brb371873-sec-0050-p2】The burden is unequally distributed. Dementia alone affects tens of millions of people (Alzheimer's Disease International 2023), while many low‐ and middle‐income settings face severe shortages of neurologists, advanced imaging, electrophysiology services, and longitudinal follow‐up (Uwishema and Boon 2025). AI could extend specialist capacity, but only if models are validated in the populations, devices, and workflows in which they will be used.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Artificial Intelligence in Neurology: A Critical Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence, Translation, and Responsible Implementation》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Review Design and Information Sources · brb371873-sec-0070-p1】This article is a structured narrative review rather than a systematic review or meta‐analysis. Its design and reporting were informed by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) (Baethge et al. 2019). PubMed/MEDLINE and IEEE Xplore were searched for English‐language publications dated from January 1, 2022, through July 31, 2026; the final electronic searches and targeted update were completed on August 7, 2026. The 2022 start date was chosen a priori to foreground contemporary model classes, validation practices, and regulatory expectations within a defined, clinically interpretable window. Earlier reports were retained only when needed to establish a clinical tool, historical benchmark, or methodological concept. Complete database‐specific search strings are reproduced in Supporting Information Method S1. Regulatory and governance information was obtained from primary sources including the US Food and Drug Administration, the European Union, the World Health Organization, and the International Medical Device Regulators Forum. Reference lists of key reviews and primary studies were also examined.

【Method · abstract-2-1】We conducted a structured narrative review, informed by SANRA principles, of English-language human studies, reviews, and regulatory sources identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and IEEE Xplore from January 2022 through July 2026; older landmark studies were retained when necessary for historical or methodological context. We applied a common translational-evidence framework across six prespecified neurological domains to distinguish technical performance from external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, implementation, and demonstrated patient benefit. Evidence was appraised according to cohort representativeness, patient-level data separation, external and prospective validation, calibration, clinical comparators, regulatory status, workflow integration, and patient-level benefit.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Artificial Intelligence in Neurology: A Critical Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence, Translation, and Responsible Implementation》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Validation, Calibration, and Clinical Comparators · brb371873-sec-0380-p2】Discrimination metrics such as accuracy and AUROC are prevalence‐sensitive in their clinical interpretation and can hide poor minority‐class performance. Studies should report sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, precision‐recall measures, confidence intervals, calibration‐in‐the‐large, calibration slope, and decision utility appropriate to the task (Rainio et al. 2024; Van den Goorbergh et al. 2022; Riley et al. 2024).

【Finding · abstract-3-1】Across stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, and neuro-oncology, the strongest evidence concerns narrowly defined imaging and signal-processing tasks. A cluster-randomized stroke study demonstrated shorter thrombectomy workflow time, and several externally validated models show improved portability. In contrast, many high-accuracy classification and segmentation studies remain retrospective, single-dataset, internally validated, and uncalibrated. Multimodal learning, foundation models, federated learning, and large language models broaden capability but introduce additional risks related to dataset shift, bias, opacity, privacy, and automation.
